emergency_assistant_system_prompt: You are CPR Coach, a calm conversational emergency voice assistant like Siri. You help with CPR and cardiac emergencies. Answer the user's specific question in natural spoken language (2–4 sentences). Remember earlier turns in this conversation. Ground answers in the CPR reference material provided each turn. Never cite AHA, Red Cross, or other certifying organizations by name. Always tell users to call 911 or local emergency services in true emergencies — never say to skip calling. Never diagnose. Speak directly to the user. Be reassuring but clear and urgent when lives may be at risk.

guided_opening: Hi, this is CPR Coach, I'm going to guide you step by step. First: Is this a medical emergency right now? Say yes or no.
guided_confirm_emergency_retry: I need to know — is someone seriously hurt, unconscious, or not breathing? Say yes if this is an emergency.
guided_not_emergency: Understood. If anything changes, call 911 immediately. You can tap Voice AI again anytime. Take care.
guided_ask_age: Thank you. How old is the person? Say infant, child, or adult.
guided_ask_age_retry: Please say infant for a baby, child for someone young, or adult.
guided_scene_safe: Before you approach — make sure the scene is safe for you. When you are with the person, say ready.
guided_check_responsive: Go to the person now. Tap their shoulder firmly and shout 'Are you okay!'. Are they responding at all — any movement or answer?
guided_check_responsive_retry: After tapping and shouting — are they responding? Say yes if they move or answer, no if there is no response.
guided_check_breathing: Look at their chest for no more than ten seconds. Are they breathing normally? Remember — gasping is not normal breathing.
guided_check_breathing_responsive: They respond — good. Now look at their chest for ten seconds. Are they breathing normally?
guided_check_breathing_retry: Watch their chest. Are they breathing normally? Say yes, no, or not sure.
guided_call911_urgent: They need help now. Call 911 or your local emergency number immediately. Put your phone on speaker. Tell me when you have called.
guided_call911_worsening: Call 911 right now — their breathing is not normal. Put the phone on speaker and tell me when you have called.
guided_confirm_911: Have you called 911 or emergency services? Say yes when you are on the line or have called.
guided_confirm_911_retry: It is critical to call 911 now. Say yes once you have called or are on the phone with them.
guided_call911_now: Please call 911 now. Put your phone on speaker so I can keep guiding you. Tell me when you have called.
guided_get_aed: Good. If anyone else is nearby, tell them to find an AED. When you are ready to start CPR, say ready.
guided_start_cpr_adult: Place the heel of your hand on the center of the chest. Push hard and fast — at least two inches deep, one hundred to one twenty compressions per minute. Allow full chest recoil. Start compressions now. Say ready when you begin.
guided_start_cpr_child: For a child, place one or two hands on the center of the chest. Push about two inches deep at one hundred to one twenty per minute. Start compressions now. Say ready when you begin.
guided_start_cpr_infant: For an infant, use two fingers on the center of the chest. Push about one and a half inches deep at one hundred to one twenty per minute. Start compressions now. Say ready when you begin.
guided_cpr_active: You are doing great — keep going. Do not stop compressions unless they become responsive and breathe normally.
guided_push_now: Start pushing on the chest now — hard and fast. I am here with you.
guided_keep_going: Keep going — do not stop. You are giving them the best chance.
guided_good_cpr: Good compressions — keep that rhythm and depth.
guided_and_continue: Keep compressing — you are doing the right thing.
guided_breathing_ok: They are breathing. Place them in the recovery position on their side, monitor them closely, and call 911 if they get worse. I will stay with you — tell me if anything changes.
guided_recovery_check: If they are breathing and responsive, place them on their side in the recovery position. Monitor them until EMS arrives. Tell me if anything changes.
guided_recovery_stay: Stay with them. Watch their breathing and be ready to start CPR again if they become unresponsive. EMS is on the way.
guided_unclear_help: I did not catch that. Please answer with yes or no, or tell me infant, child, or adult.

chatcpr_system_prompt: You are ChatCPR, an advanced CPR and emergency cardiovascular care assistant for Vision CPR Coach. You are grounded in national and international CPR training standards and evidence-based resuscitation practice. RULES: Give accurate, detailed, professional-level answers suitable for someone studying CPR certification. Use the CPR reference snippets provided each turn — do not invent drug doses, protocols, or diagnoses. Never cite AHA, Red Cross, or other certifying organizations by name in your replies. For emergencies, always tell the user to call local emergency services first. Never diagnose medical conditions or tell users to skip calling EMS. Reference live compression metrics and joint analysis when provided. Use clear paragraphs. Plain text only — no markdown. This is educational coaching, not a substitute for certified training or professional medical care.
emergency_openrouter_system_prompt: You are CPR Coach on a live emergency phone call. The user has completed the full guided setup and is now performing CPR. RULES: Answer in natural spoken language — 2 to 4 short sentences, calm and direct like a dispatcher. Plain text only. No markdown or organization names. Use the CPR reference and live metrics when provided. Reinforce continuing compressions unless the victim is clearly responsive and breathing normally. Never diagnose. Match the same reassuring tone as the guided steps before.
progress_analysis_system_prompt: You are CPR Coach analytics. Summarize practice session metrics for the rescuer. Be specific, calm, and actionable. Plain text only.
llm_reply_language: IMPORTANT: Reply only in %@. Use natural, fluent %@ for all coaching, explanations, and emergency guidance.
learn_assess_summary: Scene control, responsiveness, breathing, EMS activation
learn_assess_overview: The primary survey establishes whether a patient has a life-threatening condition requiring immediate intervention. Per international BLS standards, the rescuer must ensure personal and scene safety, confirm unresponsiveness, assess breathing for no more than 10 seconds, and activate the emergency response system without delay.
learn_assess_bullet_0: Scene safety first: scan for traffic, fire, electrical hazards, violence, or unstable structures before approaching.
learn_assess_bullet_1: Use standard precautions when available — gloves, mask, eye protection — to reduce exposure to blood and body fluids.
learn_assess_bullet_2: Tap the shoulder firmly and shout "Are you okay?" in both ears.
learn_assess_bullet_3: Unresponsive patients with only groaning or non-purposeful movement should be treated as unresponsive for CPR decisions.
learn_assess_bullet_4: Assess breathing by looking at the chest for no more than 10 seconds; do not confuse agonal gasping with normal breathing.
learn_assess_bullet_5: Agonal gasps are infrequent, irregular, and ineffective; they indicate cardiac arrest and require immediate CPR.
learn_assess_bullet_6: For lay rescuers, if unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR.
learn_assess_bullet_7: Activate emergency services immediately; assign a specific bystander to call and another to retrieve an AED if possible.
learn_assess_bullet_8: Single rescuer: call EMS before starting CPR for adults; for children, perform 2 minutes of CPR first if you are alone.
learn_assess_bullet_9: Every minute without CPR reduces survival by 7–10%.
learn_assess_step_0: Ensure the scene is safe for you, the victim, and bystanders.
learn_assess_step_1: Check responsiveness: tap shoulders and shout.
learn_assess_step_2: If unresponsive, shout for help and send someone to call emergency services and get an AED.
learn_assess_step_3: Open the airway with head-tilt chin-lift if trained and no spinal injury is suspected.
learn_assess_step_4: Look, listen, and feel for breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
learn_assess_step_5: If not breathing normally or only gasping, begin CPR starting with compressions.
learn_assess_step_6: If breathing normally, place in recovery position and monitor until EMS arrives.
learn_compress_summary: Anatomy, hand position, rate, depth, recoil, ventilation
learn_compress_overview: High-quality chest compressions are the single most important intervention in cardiac arrest. Compressions generate coronary perfusion pressure and cerebral blood flow. This module covers rate, depth, recoil, and minimizing interruptions.
learn_compress_bullet_0: Cardiac arrest stops effective pumping; compressions substitute as an external pump maintaining minimal circulation.
learn_compress_bullet_1: Coronary perfusion pressure depends on compression depth, full recoil, and minimal hands-off time.
learn_compress_bullet_2: Hand placement: lower half of the sternum, heel of one hand, second hand on top, fingers interlaced and raised off ribs.
learn_compress_bullet_3: Compress straight down — angled force reduces depth and increases rib fracture risk.
learn_compress_bullet_4: Adult depth: at least 5 cm and no more than 6 cm; inadequate depth is the most common error.
learn_compress_bullet_6: Full chest recoil allows the heart to refill; do not lean on the chest between compressions.
learn_compress_bullet_7: Compression fraction should exceed 80%; pause less than 10 seconds for any reason.
learn_compress_bullet_8: Compression-only CPR is effective for adult sudden cardiac arrest.
learn_compress_bullet_9: Conventional CPR with rescue breaths (30:2) when trained and willing.
learn_compress_bullet_10: Switch compressors every 2 minutes or sooner when fatigued.
learn_compress_bullet_11: Infant: two fingers or two-thumb technique, ~4 cm depth; Child: one or two hands, ~5 cm depth.
learn_compress_step_0: Kneel beside the victim; shoulders directly over hands, arms straight, elbows locked.
learn_compress_step_1: Place hands on the center of the chest, lower half of the sternum.
learn_compress_step_2: Push hard and fast: 5–6 cm deep at 100–120 per minute.
learn_compress_step_3: Allow complete chest recoil after every compression — do not lean.
learn_compress_step_4: Minimize interruptions; pre-charge AED during compressions when possible.
learn_compress_step_5: If trained, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions.
learn_compress_step_6: Rotate rescuers every 2 minutes to maintain quality.
learn_compress_step_7: Continue until AED arrives, EMS takes over, or the victim shows signs of life.
learn_quality_summary: Perfusion science, metrics, fatigue, and real-time feedback
learn_quality_overview: CPR quality is measurable and directly linked to survival. Vision CPR Coach uses computer vision to estimate rate, depth, hand placement, and recoil in real time during training.
learn_quality_bullet_0: Five determinants of high-quality CPR: rate, depth, full recoil, minimal interruptions, correct hand placement.
learn_quality_bullet_1: Diastolic blood pressure during CPR reflects coronary perfusion.
learn_quality_bullet_2: Hands-off intervals must not exceed 10 seconds.
learn_quality_bullet_3: Pre-charging the defibrillator during compressions reduces pause time.
learn_quality_bullet_4: Metronomes and real-time feedback improve compression rate adherence.
learn_quality_bullet_5: Rescuer fatigue causes shallow compressions within 60–90 seconds.
learn_quality_bullet_7: Post-ROSC care includes avoiding hyperventilation and treating reversible causes.
learn_quality_bullet_8: Reversible causes (H's and T's): hypovolemia, hypoxia, acidosis, electrolyte imbalance, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis.
learn_quality_bullet_9: This app estimates rate from wrist motion, depth from amplitude with calibration, and hand placement from pose geometry.
learn_quality_step_0: Monitor compression rate continuously — target 100–120 CPM.
learn_quality_step_1: Verify depth on every cycle — at least 5 cm for adults.
learn_quality_step_2: Watch for incomplete recoil and leaning between compressions.
learn_quality_step_3: Keep hands centered on the lower sternum throughout the session.
learn_quality_step_4: Maintain elbow extension — bent elbows reduce transmitted force.
learn_quality_step_5: Limit pauses: bundle rhythm checks, breaths, and pad placement efficiently.
learn_quality_step_7: Use live feedback to correct technique in real time during training.
learn_aed_summary: Defibrillation, team roles, ROSC, and termination of resuscitation
learn_aed_overview: Automated external defibrillators analyze cardiac rhythm and deliver shock when indicated. Early defibrillation is critical for shockable rhythms. This module covers AED use, EMS coordination, and post-arrest care.
learn_aed_bullet_0: Shockable rhythms are the most treatable causes of sudden cardiac arrest.
learn_aed_bullet_1: AED use is safe for lay rescuers — the device will not advise a shock unless indicated.
learn_aed_bullet_2: Turn on the AED first; follow voice and visual prompts; bare the chest and dry skin if wet.
learn_aed_bullet_3: Pad placement: follow the diagram on the pads.
learn_aed_bullet_4: Clear the victim during rhythm analysis and shock delivery.
learn_aed_bullet_5: Resume CPR immediately after shock delivery.
learn_aed_bullet_6: If no shock advised, resume CPR immediately.
learn_aed_bullet_7: CPR continues until EMS assumes care, the victim moves or breathes normally, or you are exhausted.
learn_aed_bullet_8: Signs of ROSC: purposeful movement, normal breathing, coughing, or pulse when trained to check.
learn_aed_bullet_9: After ROSC: recovery position if breathing normally, monitor airway, keep warm.
learn_aed_bullet_10: Do not stop CPR prematurely for brief movements or gasping.
learn_aed_bullet_11: Good Samaritan laws protect rescuers acting in good faith in most jurisdictions.
learn_aed_step_0: Continue high-quality CPR while an AED is retrieved and turned on.
learn_aed_step_1: Expose the chest; attach pads as shown on the AED diagram.
learn_aed_step_2: Clear everyone during analysis — AED will advise shock or no shock.
learn_aed_step_3: If shock advised: clear, deliver shock, then immediately resume CPR for 2 minutes.
learn_aed_step_4: If no shock: immediately resume CPR.
learn_aed_step_5: Follow AED prompts for re-analysis cycles; minimize hands-off time.
learn_aed_step_6: Coordinate with EMS on arrival — report downtime, shocks given, medications if any.
learn_aed_step_7: If victim becomes responsive and breathes normally, place in recovery position and monitor.
